items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> dreads standing guard all night at the <radical>ceremony</radical>. They stuff a coat with straw and lean it against the post instead. Nobody notices the swap, and the dummy becomes their <kanji>substitute</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Dai, the giant baby, truck-sized, toddles up and spots the straw double leaned against the post. He points and wails <reading>だい</reading>, landing like the English word <reading>dye</reading> spilled across the square. The ground trembles with every sob. The straw substitute never even flinches.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A city planner caps her model tower with a stone <radical>lid</radical>. Under it she props open a stone <radical>mouth</radical> as the gate. The whole model is so <radical>small</radical> it fits in her palm, a tiny <kanji>capital</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the ceremony, a boy named <reading>Kyo</reading> knocks the whole miniature capital off the table. It shatters on the floor, and all he can do is groan <reading>きょう</reading>, one long syllable of dread, as the tiny lid and gate pieces roll under the desks.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker finds a boxy frame with crossed bars beside the trail. Curious, she puts it to <radical>use</radical>, feeding it coins for tea. Even on a bare mountain, someone found a way to <kanji>utilize</kanji> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the summit vending machine, a hiker named <reading>Yo</reading> finally gets her drink and lets out a long, relieved yodel: <reading>よう</reading>, echoing off the ridge. The machine rattles once more, empty and satisfied with its work.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Ink shoots down a <radical>slide</radical> and falls as one round <radical>drop</radical>. It splashes into a <radical>box on its side</radical> and fills it edge to edge. The ink stays penned inside, marking off its own <kanji>ward</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A pigeon named Coo waddles to the top of the slide and loses her footing. She drops straight down, cooing <reading>く</reading> the whole way, soft as an English <reading>coo</reading>. She lands smack inside the tipped-over box, wings pinned flat to its walls. Coo is boxed into her own little ward now.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A giant <radical>eye</radical> stares down at one <radical>small</radical> patch of land. It never looks away, guarding only that one stretch of ground. That single watched patch becomes its own <kanji>prefecture</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting shiba, gets posted to guard that same small patch of land under the staring eye. Every time a stranger's boot crosses the border, he barks <reading>けん</reading>, sharp as the English name <reading>Ken</reading> shouted twice. He never abandons his post. The eye above never blinks either.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>old bird</radical> refuses to fly anymore. It hops off its perch onto the winding <radical>road</radical> below. Wings folded, it walks step by step to <kanji>advance</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Watching the bird finally waddle down the road, an old walker named <reading>Shin</reading> claps once and shouts <reading>しん</reading>, cheering it on like a marathon fan. He falls in behind it, refusing to walk any faster than the bird does.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Under a <radical>cliff</radical>, a peddler takes her <radical>stand</radical> guarding a pot with a <radical>lid</radical>. A shoot of <radical>life</radical> pushes up and splits it into <radical>eight</radical> pieces. By morning her stall overflows with <kanji>products</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A customer at the stall picks up the split log and says it looks freshly <reading>sawn</reading>, <reading>さん</reading>, right down the middle. She buys every product on the counter before the sawdust even settles.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A scientist lights the first match of a brand new invention. She frames the burnt matchstick on her wall as its <radical>beginning</radical>. Visitors still point at that match as where everything had its <kanji>beginning</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the same trailhead, a hiker named <reading>Gen</reading> singes his thumb relighting that match and yelps <reading>げん</reading>, the exact sound a beginning makes when it starts with a mistake.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You balance a coin on level <radical>ground</radical>, and it tips into a <radical>slide</radical>. The coin slips down through a window where the <radical>moon</radical> hangs. It drops into your palm, and now you <kanji>possess</kanji> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the far side of that same window, a boy named <reading>Yu</reading> catches the falling coin and whoops <reading>ゆう</reading>. He stuffs it straight into his pocket and grins up at the moon, already counting the coin as his.

items.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting shiba, patrols the fresh foundation line like it is one more sword for his wall. Every lap he barks <reading>けん</reading>, and the crew swears the dog is shouting his own name, <reading>Ken</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You lean against a gate stuck at a dead <radical>stop</radical>. A whistle cracks at dawn, and your legs launch straight into a <radical>run</radical>. You leap the gate and <kanji>rouse</kanji> yourself awake.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>big</radical> hero stands guard in a patch of <radical>grass</radical>. Rain soaks him, so his only <radical>cover</radical> is a damp blanket knotted like a cape. Freezing and proud, he still calls himself <kanji>England</kanji>.

items.description: This character originally meant outstanding or brilliant, which is why hero survives as an accepted meaning. Centuries later it was borrowed purely for its sound to write the country name England, a meaning with no real connection to the original character.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Your bare feet scorch on the baked <radical>ground</radical>. You point at <radical>self</radical> and swear the heat does not bother you. Then your <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags behind, and the stubborn heat becomes <kanji>summer</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, sags on a power line above that same baked ground. Too hot even for him, he cracks his beak and a weak puff of flame escapes with a scorched <reading>か</reading>. That tired flame-cough is how you remember summer's reading, <reading>か</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: You <radical>stand</radical> at the edge of a <radical>cliff</radical> holding a pot <radical>lid</radical> full of paint. You dab <radical>three</radical> quick streaks onto a giant stone <radical>head</radical> beside you. Those streaks blink open into a grinning <kanji>face</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back on the cliff edge, a photographer named <reading>Gan</reading> leans in too close for the shot and slips on loose gravel. He yelps a sharp <reading>がん</reading> as he grabs the rock ledge, dangling right below the sleepy head on the page.

items.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>arrow</radical> hits a target and snaps in half, the pieces splitting apart like <radical>eight</radical>. The stub falls into a bowl of <radical>beans</radical> and looks tiny beside a whole one. Cut off before its time, the little arrow stays <kanji>short</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The vendor is a wiry guy everyone calls <reading>Tan</reading>. Every time he pulls another snapped stub from the bowl, he mutters <reading>たん</reading> under his breath. He's annoyed at how short his profits look today.
items.description: Beyond literal shortness, 短 also carries the sense of a shortcoming. It's the kind of short that comes up when someone lists a personality flaw or weak point, not just a measurement of length.

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は時間がとても短いです。
example_sentences.english: There isn't much time today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は時[じ]間[かん]がとても短[みじか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: この道は短いです。

example_sentences.furigana: この道[みち]は短[みじか]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 妹の髪は短いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> who can <radical>renew</radical> anything for you without leaving the counter is selling pure <kanji>convenience</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The badger's slam sends the vending machine's change chute rattling out coins. The hiker who planned to buy one — a guy named <reading>Ben</reading> — just mutters 「<reading>べん</reading>」 under his breath, resigned to waiting outside in the rain.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A curved hill holds a setting moon, sliced by one falling line. The light fades to blue as hush settles into <radical>evening</radical>. This whole little picture simply means <kanji>evening</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Seki comes out onto his step at this hour every night, and you hear him before you see him — that wet, rattling 「<reading>せき</reading>」 of a cough carrying right down the street. When せき starts up, the light has gone.

items.reading_mnemonic: The butcher, whose name tag just says <reading>Nick</reading>, finally chases the cat off with a broom, growling <reading>にく</reading> at it like a curse word. He rehangs the swinging slabs and locks the frame before the cat tries its luck again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The plaza of <radical>earth</radical> is held in high <radical>esteem</radical> by the whole town. A crowd fills it, too big for the open sky above. Someone stretches a giant <radical>cover</radical> across it, and it becomes the <kanji>public chamber</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Under the same blanket-roofed hall, a baker elbows in holding a fresh lump of <reading>dough</reading>, insisting the shrine crowd taste it. Everyone groans one long <reading>どう</reading>, half hunger, half surrender, and makes room for him anyway.
items.description: This kanji almost never stands alone. In real use it is nearly always the second half of a compound naming one specific large room — a dining hall, a lecture hall — rather than a generic public chamber on its own.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A clumsy <radical>bird</radical> waddles into the convenience store, wings tucked like it is cold. It flops onto the rice ball shelf with a thud. The clerk sighs and carries the <kanji>bird</kanji> back outside.
items.reading_mnemonic: Everyone at the konbini calls the night clerk <reading>Chow</reading>. He barks <reading>ちょう</reading> at the bird every single night, like he's calling a stray in for dinner. It never once listens.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>drop</radical> hangs frozen off the fence, refusing to fall. The same cold locks your <radical>trailing foot</radical> in mid-step. Everything holds still in the grip of <kanji>winter</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at that fence, a shivering dog named Toby paws at his own frozen <reading>toe</reading> and yelps <reading>とう</reading>, breath crystallizing mid-air just like the drop dangling above him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>dog</radical> spins in tight circles on the porch, chasing an itch on its own tail. It keeps spinning without ever catching it. Finally it flops down panting, every inch a stubborn <kanji>dog</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still panting on the shrine steps, the dog corners into <reading>Ken</reading>, the shiba who guards a wall of antique swords. Ken plants himself between the blades and the newcomer, barking a short, sharp <reading>けん</reading> that echoes off the mossy stone.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Through the window you watch the <radical>sun</radical> blaze over the crosswalk. An <radical>old</radical> man shuffles across without hurrying for anyone. The asphalt shimmers in the thick <kanji>sultry</kanji> air.
items.reading_mnemonic: The kid waiting beside him is named <reading>Sho</reading>. He wilts in the heat and groans <reading>しょ</reading> under his breath. He wishes the old man would hurry so the signal would finally let him escape the sun.
items.description: This kanji is only used for the sultry heat of weather or air: a stifling afternoon, a muggy room. It never describes a hot object, a hot drink, or a fever. Those use a different word entirely.

example_sentences.furigana: 夏[なつ]はいつも暑[あつ]いです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Snow buries the <radical>roof</radical> of the village <radical>well</radical>. A <radical>drop</radical> from the bucket rope freezes solid before it falls. Someone splits firewood into <radical>eight</radical> pieces, but the <kanji>cold</kanji> yard stays frozen anyway.
items.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Khan</reading> comes to fill his bucket at that same frozen well. His fingers touch the ice and he yelps <reading>かん</reading>, yanking his hand back and blowing on it. His shivering bark echoes off the roof above.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>big</radical> man kneels on the <radical>ground</radical> beside a river of <radical>water</radical>. He plants <radical>two</radical> stalks of <radical>grass</radical> in it and opens his <radical>mouth</radical> to sing. His song names this whole land <kanji>China</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: By the river, the scholar seals his finished scroll inside a battered tin <reading>can</reading> to keep out the damp. He raps the lid twice and it rings out <reading>かん</reading>, <reading>かん</reading>, echoing over the water. That hollow knock is the sound stamped on every character he writes.
items.description: 漢 rarely stands by itself. It usually works as a bound prefix meaning Chinese or Sino-, attached ahead of another kanji rather than standing alone. In some older compounds the same character can also simply mean "a man" or "fellow," with no connection to China at all.
